CHAP. I.
1. Iu the beginuing. ) Holie Moyfes telleth what was done in the beginning of
the world, and ſo forward euen til hit owne time, writing aboue two thouſand
and toure hundreth veares after the beg inning. Al which being incom prehenſible
by humane wit or diſcourſe, he knew partly by reuelations from God, fot he had
the guift of Prophecic in toſt excellent ſort: partly by traditions from his elders,
who learned of their fathers. For vntil that time the Church had only traditions
ot ſuch things as were reuealed to ſpecial men, whereby we fee the great autho-
rity of traditious, bef ore thtre were Scriptures. Aud ſince Scriptures were writ-
ten they are alſo neceſſary, for three ſpecial teaſons. Firſt, for that we are only
aſſured by tradition of the Church, that thoſe books are indeed holy Scriptures,
which are fo accounted, and not by the Scripture it- felfe, for that were to proue
the ſame by the ſame, vntil we be affured of ſome part, that proueth ſome other
parts. And this made S. Auguſtin to ſay plainly, that he culd not belieue the Ghoſpel,
exceot the Churth told hiu which it the Ghoſpel. Secondlly, holy Scriptures being once
knowen to be the word of God, & ſo of moſt eminent authoritie of al writings in
the world, as S. Auguſtin, S Hicrome, & al other Fathers agree, yet for the true vn-
derſtanding of the ſame, both the Scripture it-ſelte, and the ancient Fathers remit
vs to the Church, namely to thoſe in the Church that are aypointed bv Gods ordt-
nance, in the hich place that he hath choſen. Which were the High Prieſts in the old
Teſtament, as appeareth Deut. 17. Mat. 23. Ioan. 11. And in the new Teſtament,
S. Peter & his Succeſtours, for whom Chriſt prayed that his faith chould not faile:
& therfore commanded him to confirme his brethren, Luc. 22. Thirdly, for things
not expreſſed in particular in holy Scripture, the Scripture (4) & Fathers doe li-
kewife remit vs to traditions, and to the iudgement & teſtimonie of the Church.
Chriſt ſaying to his Apoſtles : te that beareib vou heareth me. The Apoſtles doubted
not to ſay: It feemed good to the Holie Ghoſt and to vt. And S. Paul willed the Theſta-
lonians to hold the traduiont, which they had learned, whether it were by word, or by
his Epiſtle.

ſignification of the words, as the letter inay ſeem to ſound, but expound al allego-
rically, as that by the waters aboue the firmament should be vnderſtood the blefſed
Angels, by the watert vnder the firmament wicked ſpirits, and the like. So did
Origen and diuers that follow him therein. Yea S. Auguſtin in his books vpon Ge-
neſis againſt the Manichees, written shortlv after his conuerſion, when he could
not find as he deſired a good and probable ſenſe agreable to the words in their
proper ſignification, expounded them myſtically , but afterwards in his other
books de Geneſi ad literam, he gratefully acknowledgeth that God had giuen
hitn fur thet ſight therin, and tha: now he ſuppofed he could interprete al accor-
ding to the proper ſignification of the words: yet ſo that he durſt not nor would
not add ict himſelfe to one ſenſe, but that he was readie to imbrace another, Icſt by
ſticking to his owne iudgement he might faile. So likewi ſe S. Baſil, S. Chriſoſtom,
S. Ambroſe, S. Hierome, S. Bede, and other gre ateſt Doctours found and confeſſed
